original_question: Which components of observed post-burst gamma-ray-burst light curves are genuinely produced by the external forward or reverse shock, and how should jet breaks, chromatic behavior, and reverse-shock signatures be interpreted once internal central-engine contributions are removed? This is especially important in the Swift era, where X-ray afterglows commonly contain multiple components that complicate standard external-shock parameter inference.
target_in_paper: In the Swift era, the afterglow modeling made one step backwards: instead of constraining the afterglow model parameters using the data, one needs first to identify which emission component is from the external forward shock, and which is not.
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the need to determine which afterglow components originate from the external forward shock and reverse shock, highlights the role of jet breaks and chromatic behaviors, and notes the contamination of X-ray afterglows by internal engine emission in the Swift era.
missing_details: Definition of the canonical X-ray afterglow lightcurve components I–V (early steep decay, shallow decay, normal decay, late steep decay, X-ray flares) as per Nousek et al. [125,126]

Specification that components I and V are internal (prompt steep decay and flares) and components II–IV are attributed to external shock phases (continuous energy injection, post-injection decay, and jet break)

Definition of the standard external forward shock model free parameters: isotropic-equivalent blastwave energy E_iso, circumburst medium density (n for ISM or A* for wind), electron power-law index p, electron equipartition fraction ε_e, and magnetic equipartition fraction ε_B
Definition of reverse shock emission: its origin in the ejecta, expected IR/optical/UV peak, characteristic double-peaked optical lightcurve, and dependence on ejecta magnetization σ
Clarification of 'jet break' as a hydrodynamical achromatic break predicted by the external-shock model and the notion of a 'platinum jet break'
Clarification of achromatic versus chromatic breaks across X-ray and optical bands
Clarification that multi-wavelength (radio, optical, X-ray) observations are required to identify external-shock components
Explanation of internal (central-engine) contributions including internal plateaus and X-ray flares that must be subtracted
refined_question: In Swift-era gamma-ray burst afterglows, the observed X-ray lightcurve typically consists of five segments: (I) an early steep decay and (V) late-time X-ray flares, both attributed to internal central-engine dissipation, sandwiched around segments (II) shallow decay (plateau), (III) normal decay, and (IV) a late steep decay often associated with a jet break. Once the internal steep-decay and flare components are removed, which of the remaining X-ray and contemporaneous optical/infrared features — including the plateau, normal-decay, late-steep-decay segments, and any reverse-shock optical signatures — can be unambiguously identified as arising from the external forward shock and the reverse shock within the standard external-shock model (characterized by the isotropic-equivalent kinetic energy E_iso, circumburst medium density, electron spectral index p, and energy-partition fractions ε_e and ε_B)? Furthermore, how should (a) the presence or absence of an achromatic late-time jet-break signature, (b) the occurrence of chromatic breaks between X-ray and optical bands, and (c) the diversity of reverse-shock optical emission profiles — including their sensitivity to ejecta magnetization parameter σ and ejecta stratification — be interpreted in the external-shock framework after subtraction of all internal engine contributions?
justification: The refined question directly extracts the open problem described in Section 2.8 of the paper, which emphasizes that in the Swift era one must distinguish genuine external-shock emission from internal central-engine contributions before fitting the external-shock model parameters (Section 2.8, p. 215 lines 554–556). It expands the draft by specifying the five canonical X-ray afterglow components (I–V) and identifies which are internal, incorporates the definitions of the standard forward-shock model parameters [196,286–288], defines jet breaks as achromatic hydrodynamical breaks [293,294], clarifies achromatic versus chromatic behavior [266,129,90], and includes reverse-shock emission properties and their dependence on ejecta magnetization σ [162,163], all of which are essential to pose the question in a self-contained, paper-faithful manner.
